Part 0

Getting started

README.md

Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning — theory, mathematics, and code

For the requested RL syllabus, start with the RL coverage and prerequisites guide.

Start with the theory and code index, then follow the learning map. Every one of the 31 lesson scripts has a matching Markdown chapter beside it: for example, 06_ppo_and_gae.md explains the mathematics behind 06_ppo_and_gae.py.

Read the chapter first for intuition, definitions, derivations, worked numerical examples, and a map from equations to code. Then run and modify the Python file. Start with the math primer if derivatives, expectations, entropy, or KL divergence are unfamiliar.

This is a broad beginner-to-advanced foundation, not an exhaustive treatment of every research method. Complete trainers and isolated equation labs are clearly identified. Small toy successes are not evidence of real-world model quality.

Setup

Use Python 3.11 or newer. Run these commands in this folder:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python 01_foundations/01_python_and_math.py
python 01_foundations/02_tensors_autograd.py

On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate instead. For a CPU-only PyTorch installation on Linux/Windows, you can use python -m pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu. For CUDA, follow the PyTorch installation selector. No GPU or account is needed for the core lessons. The first Python/math lesson, bandits, value iteration, Q-learning/SARSA, and bootstrap evaluation need only Python.

Folder What you learn

Read matching .md and .py files together in numerical order within each folder. The real-model scripts are optional: you can continue into RL without downloading any pretrained model.

Run and check the offline lessons

python run_lessons.py --list
python run_lessons.py --stdlib-only
python run_lessons.py
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

The runner excludes external model downloads and the multi-process DDP lesson. It runs each lesson separately with a timeout and reports failures. To run DDP:

torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 05_advanced/07_distributed_training.py

Fine-tune an actual pretrained model

python -m pip install -r requirements-huggingface.txt
python 02_finetuning/04_huggingface_sft.py --model sshleifer/tiny-gpt2 --steps 5
python 02_finetuning/05_reload_and_generate.py
# A larger pretrained base, still small by LLM standards:
python 02_finetuning/04_huggingface_sft.py --model distilgpt2 --method lora --steps 20
# Full parameter fine-tuning:
python 02_finetuning/04_huggingface_sft.py --method full --output outputs/full

The tiny GPT-2 option checks the pipeline; expect poor generated text. Even DistilGPT-2 with eight teaching examples will not become a useful assistant. First runs require internet and disk space for model downloads. CPU training of the larger model is slower and requires more RAM. Outputs are saved locally, never uploaded. Select a new --output directory to preserve previous runs.

For the optional NVIDIA GPU QLoRA branch, install bitsandbytes, then add --qlora --method lora. That branch is hardware-dependent. Larger model choices need a compatible tokenizer/template and enough GPU memory. QLoRA support is based on the Transformers quantization documentation.

How to study a file

  1. Read the matching Markdown chapter and derive its worked example by hand.
  2. Open the Python file and connect each main operation to its equation.
  3. Predict the tensor shapes and output before running it.
  4. Run once, then change one hyperparameter and record the result.
  5. Complete the exercise in the comments. Explain why the result changed.
  6. Reimplement the central equation without looking, then compare.

Keep an experiment journal: hypothesis, seed, configuration, data split, metrics, failure cases, and conclusion. Consult tricks and debugging, the glossary, and primary sources. See verification details for what was actually executed.

00_start/LEARNING_MAP.md

A practical learning map

Every lesson now has a matching .md explanation and .py implementation. Use the paired index to read theory before code. For notation and mathematical prerequisites, see the math primer.

Prerequisites: basic computer use and willingness to read Python. The first lesson introduces lists, functions, loops, dot products, softmax and derivatives; if those are completely new, pause and practice each with your own numbers. You do not need to know deep learning before starting.

Stage 1: Learn what training actually does

Read 01_foundations/01 through 03. Understand a prediction, loss, derivative, parameter update, minibatch, and held-out evaluation. Derive the two gradients in linear regression by hand. Explain why removing all nonlinearities makes a multilayer network equivalent to one linear map.

Checkpoint: fit a different synthetic function and explain training versus validation performance without using the word “magic.”

Stage 2: Understand language models

Read foundations 04 and 05. Trace text -> token IDs -> embeddings -> causal attention -> logits -> next-token loss. Track [batch, sequence, vocabulary] shapes. Distinguish pretraining from fine-tuning and inference.

Checkpoint: explain why a causal model cannot see tomorrow's target token, why generation repeatedly calls the model, and what temperature changes.

Stage 3: Fine-tune responsibly and efficiently

Read all files in 02_finetuning. Start with a source/target task, then learn response-only supervision and LoRA algebra. Use the external model workflow only after understanding the offline versions. Read the saved adapter config and identify which original base weights are needed for reload.

Checkpoint: explain the difference between the attention mask and label mask; show that frozen parameters do not change; compare full tuning and LoRA at the same evaluation budget. QLoRA means a quantized frozen base plus trainable adapters.

Stage 4: Learn RL from small environments

Read 03_reinforcement_learning in order. Distinguish reward (one step) from return (discounted future sum). Compute a Bellman backup by hand. Move from a table to a neural Q function, then to an explicitly stochastic policy.

Checkpoint: explain on-policy versus off-policy, why replay helps DQN but stale replay is problematic for ordinary PPO, and why termination differs from a collector's time limit. Explain why GAE uses two different masks.

Stage 5: Connect LLM fine-tuning to preference optimization

Read 04_alignment. SFT imitates demonstrations. A reward model learns pairwise preferences. RLHF optimizes generated behavior against rewards and a reference constraint. DPO learns directly from fixed preference pairs. GRPO compares multiple sampled answers to the same prompt without a learned value critic.

Checkpoint: trace which tensors receive gradients. Explain the separate roles of the reference policy and the old rollout policy. They are NOT interchangeable. The alignment examples use tiny feature/categorical problems to expose the objectives; they do not implement production LLM alignment pipelines.

Stage 6: Study advanced objectives and systems

Read 05_advanced. Reproduce each equation before extending it. SAC and CQL are explicit equation labs; extend them into full agents only after understanding replay collection, target updates, evaluation, and environment action bounds. Read the roadmap below for subjects that require separate larger projects.

Checkpoint: distinguish memory for parameters, gradients, optimizer states, and activations. Explain how mixed precision, LoRA, checkpointing, DDP and FSDP address different parts of the problem.

00_start/RL_COVERAGE.md

Requested RL syllabus: prerequisites, mathematics, and code

Start here to study the requested topics. Paths are relative to this file; run commands from the finetuning_and_rl folder. Core code is offline and CPU-sized.

Prerequisite sequence

  1. Python loops, functions, lists, classes, random sampling, and numerical debugging: Python and math.
  2. Sums, vectors/matrices, conditional probability, expectations, variance, derivatives/chain rule, softmax, logarithms, entropy and KL: math primer. Practice each short calculation there.
  3. Tensors, gradients, gradient descent and loss functions: autograd and neural network training.
  4. For deep RL: function approximation and optimizer behavior. For TRPO add Hessians and solving linear systems; its chapter introduces local curvature.
  5. For GRPO and self-distillation: token/attention basics, causal language modeling, and response masking.

RL setup and the difference between an MDP and RL

An MDP is a mathematical problem specification M=(S,A,P,R,γ,ρ0)\mathcal M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,P,R,\gamma,\rho_0)M=(S,A,P,R,γ,ρ0​): states, actions, transition law, expected reward, discount, and initial-state distribution. The Markov property is P(St+1,rt∣S0,A0,…,St,At)=P(St+1,rt∣St,At)P(S_{t+1},r_t\mid S_0,A_0,\ldots,S_t,A_t)=P(S_{t+1},r_t\mid S_t,A_t)P(St+1​,rt​∣S0​,A0​,…,St​,At​)=P(St+1​,rt​∣St​,At​). RL is a learning framework: an agent uses experience to improve decisions, frequently without knowing PPP or RRR. An MDP may be solved by planning with a known model; RL may learn a model or learn values/policies directly. A partially observed agent generally needs history or belief state rather than the raw observation.

S0∼ρ0,At∼πθ(⋅∣St),(St+1,rt)∼p(⋅,⋅∣St,At),S_0\sim\rho_0,\quad A_t\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid S_t),\quad (S_{t+1},r_t)\sim p(\cdot,\cdot\mid S_t,A_t),S0​∼ρ0​,At​∼πθ​(⋅∣St​),(St+1​,rt​)∼p(⋅,⋅∣St​,At​),

J(θ)=Eπθ[∑t=0T−1γtrt].J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t r_t\right]. J(θ)=Eπθ​​[t=0∑T−1​γtrt​].

Here rtr_trt​ denotes the reward received after action AtA_tAt​; some books call it Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​. Define Vπ(s)=E[Gt∣St=s]V^\pi(s)=E[G_t\mid S_t=s]Vπ(s)=E[Gt​∣St​=s], Qπ(s,a)=E[Gt∣St=s,At=a]Q^\pi(s,a)=E[G_t\mid S_t=s,A_t=a]Qπ(s,a)=E[Gt​∣St​=s,At​=a], and Aπ=Qπ−VπA^\pi=Q^\pi-V^\piAπ=Qπ−Vπ. The agent/environment loop is:

state = env.reset()
while True:
    action = agent.act(state)       # exploration is part of behavior policy
    nxt, reward, terminated, truncated = env.step(action)
    agent.observe(state, action, reward, nxt, terminated, truncated)
    if terminated or truncated:
        state = env.reset()
    else:
        state = nxt

This is interface pseudocode; the runnable lessons define their own tiny environments. A real Gymnasium reset() returns (observation, info) and step() includes an info dictionary. A true terminal suppresses bootstrap; an external continuing-task time limit bootstraps from the final observation while stopping the trace at reset. Lesson 06 implements both masks explicitly.

Model-based means using a transition model for prediction or planning; model-free means learning without that model. On-policy means targeting the behavior policy; off-policy allows a different target policy. Bootstrapping means using a learned estimate inside a target. These are separate distinctions.

00_start/MATH_PRIMER.md

The mathematical language used in this course

Read this when an equation's notation gets in the way of the idea. You do not need to memorize every identity before starting. Return to the relevant section when it first appears in a lesson.

1. Indices, sums, and shapes

xix_ixi​ means entry iii of a vector; xijx_{ij}xij​ means row iii, column jjj of a matrix. ∑i=1Nxi\sum_{i=1}^N x_i∑i=1N​xi​ means add entries 1 through NNN. Thus 1N∑ixi\frac1N\sum_i x_iN1​∑i​xi​ is their arithmetic mean. A superscript such as x2x^2x2 usually means a power, but VπV^\piVπ means “value under policy pi,” not exponentiation.

A matrix X∈RB×dX\in\mathbb R^{B\times d}X∈RB×d has BBB rows and ddd columns of real numbers. If W∈Rd×kW\in\mathbb R^{d\times k}W∈Rd×k, then XWXWXW has shape [B,k][B,k][B,k]:

(XW)ij=∑l=1dXilWlj.(XW)_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^{d}X_{il}W_{lj}. (XW)ij​=l=1∑d​Xil​Wlj​.

The transpose XTX^TXT swaps rows and columns. PyTorch's nn.Linear(d,k) stores weights as [k,d][k,d][k,d] and therefore calculates x @ weight.T + bias for row batches. Always write shapes beside an unfamiliar equation before implementing it.

2. Functions and derivatives

A function maps inputs to outputs: f(w)=w2f(w)=w^2f(w)=w2 maps 3 to 9. Its derivative f′(w)=2wf'(w)=2wf′(w)=2w describes local sensitivity. At w=3w=3w=3, a small increment hhh changes the function by approximately 6h6h6h:

f(w+h)≈f(w)+hf′(w).f(w+h)\approx f(w)+h f'(w). f(w+h)≈f(w)+hf′(w).

For several variables, a partial derivative changes one variable while holding the others fixed. The gradient stacks all partial derivatives into a vector:

∇θL=[∂L/∂θ1,…,∂L/∂θd]T.\nabla_\theta L= [\partial L/\partial\theta_1,\ldots,\partial L/\partial\theta_d]^T. ∇θ​L=[∂L/∂θ1​,…,∂L/∂θd​]T.

The chain rule differentiates a composition. If u=3wu=3wu=3w and L=u2L=u^2L=u2, then dL/dw=(dL/du)(du/dw)=2u⋅3=18wdL/dw=(dL/du)(du/dw)=2u\cdot3=18wdL/dw=(dL/du)(du/dw)=2u⋅3=18w. Backpropagation repeatedly applies this rule to a computation graph, adding contributions when a parameter affects the output through several paths.

Gradient descent is θ←θ−η∇L\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla Lθ←θ−η∇L, with learning rate η>0\eta>0η>0. Locally it moves against increasing loss. In a nonconvex network, this does not guarantee finding the global best parameters.

3. Probability and expectation

A discrete probability distribution has pi≥0p_i\ge0pi​≥0 and ∑ipi=1\sum_i p_i=1∑i​pi​=1. X∼pX\sim pX∼p means sample a random variable from distribution ppp. The expectation of a function is a probability-weighted average:

EX∼p[f(X)]=∑xp(x)f(x).\mathbb E_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\sum_x p(x)f(x). EX∼p​[f(X)]=x∑​p(x)f(x).

For rewards 0 and 1 with probabilities 0.2 and 0.8, expected reward is 0.8. A single sample is still either 0 or 1. An expectation describes an average, not what must happen on each attempt. A sample mean estimates an expectation; its reliability depends on the number and dependence of observations.

Conditional probability p(y∣x)p(y\mid x)p(y∣x) means probability of yyy given xxx. An RL policy π(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s)π(a∣s) is the action distribution conditional on state. The law of total expectation lets us average first over a next state and then over actions; this is the basis of Bellman expectation equations.

4. Logarithms, exponentials, and likelihood

Natural log and exponential are inverse functions: log⁡(eu)=u\log(e^u)=ulog(eu)=u. Products become sums: log⁡(ab)=log⁡a+log⁡b\log(ab)=\log a+\log blog(ab)=loga+logb. A sequence of conditional token probabilities multiplies to a sequence probability, but their logs add. Working in log space avoids underflow from multiplying many tiny numbers.

A likelihood treats observed data as fixed and model parameters as variable. Maximizing its log is equivalent to minimizing negative log-likelihood. For a correct class with model probability ppp, its loss is −log⁡p-\log p−logp. Probability 1 gives loss 0; probability 0.1 gives about 2.303.

Softmax converts logits ziz_izi​ into probabilities:

pi=ezi∑jezj.p_i=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}. pi​=∑j​ezj​ezi​​.

Subtracting the same constant from all logits preserves these probabilities. Subtract the maximum to improve numerical stability. See the worked softmax lesson.

5. Variance, bias, and standardization

Variance measures expected squared deviation from the mean:

Var⁡(X)=E[(X−E[X])2].\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]. Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])2].

Standard deviation is its square root. Standardization subtracts a mean and divides by a standard deviation, usually adding a tiny denominator constant for numerical stability. Standardized data is not automatically Gaussian.

For an estimator q^\hat qq^​ of qqq, bias is E[q^]−q\mathbb E[\hat q]-qE[q^​]−q. A method can be consistently wrong (bias) or fluctuate greatly (variance). Under the usual squared-error decomposition:

E[(q^−q)2]=Var⁡(q^)+(E[q^]−q)2.\mathbb E[(\hat q-q)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\hat q) +(\mathbb E[\hat q]-q)^2. E[(q^​−q)2]=Var(q^​)+(E[q^​]−q)2.

GAE trades reliance on learned value estimates against noisy observed returns. These are tendencies, not universal numeric guarantees for every parameter choice.

6. Entropy, cross-entropy, and KL divergence

For distributions ppp and qqq over the same discrete outcomes:

H(p)=−∑ipilog⁡pi,H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i, H(p)=−i∑​pi​logpi​,

H(p,q)=−∑ipilog⁡qi,H(p,q)=-\sum_i p_i\log q_i, H(p,q)=−i∑​pi​logqi​,

DKL(p∥q)=∑ipilog⁡piqi=H(p,q)−H(p).D_{KL}(p\|q)=\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}=H(p,q)-H(p). DKL​(p∥q)=i∑​pi​logqi​pi​​=H(p,q)−H(p).

Entropy measures uncertainty within ppp. Cross-entropy measures the average negative log-probability that qqq assigns to outcomes drawn from ppp. KL compares distributions and is nonnegative when well-defined, but is not a symmetric distance. If qi=0q_i=0qi​=0 where pi>0p_i>0pi​>0, KL is infinite.

For a one-hot true label, H(p)=0H(p)=0H(p)=0, so cross-entropy becomes the negative log of the predicted probability of that label. For distillation, the teacher provides a soft target distribution instead.

A sampled log-ratio log⁡(pi/qi)\log(p_i/q_i)log(pi​/qi​) can be negative. Only its expectation under ppp is constrained to be nonnegative. Continuous-action differential entropy has different properties from discrete entropy and may itself be negative.

7. Optimization versus evaluation

arg⁡max⁡af(a)\arg\max_a f(a)argmaxa​f(a) returns an input action achieving a maximum. max⁡af(a)\max_a f(a)maxa​f(a) returns the maximum value itself. Double DQN deliberately uses one network for the argmax selection and another to evaluate the selected action.

A training loss is the quantity optimized. A task metric is the quantity you care about, such as held-out correctness or episode return. They may disagree: a better reward-model score can reflect a shortcut, and a lower training loss can reflect memorization.

A stopgrad or detach operation preserves a value in the forward calculation while treating it as constant during differentiation. This distinction is central to target networks, policy-gradient advantages, and frozen teachers.

Practice before the advanced lessons

  • Compute softmax for [0,0]: answer [0.5,0.5].
  • Differentiate (2w−1)2(2w-1)^2(2w−1)2: answer 4(2w−1)4(2w-1)4(2w−1).
  • Compute expected reward for values [0,2] with probabilities [0.75,0.25]: answer 0.5.
  • Compute entropy of two equally likely outcomes: answer log⁡2≈0.693\log2\approx0.693log2≈0.693 nats.
  • For rewards [0,1] and discount 0.9, the initial return is 0.9, not 1.

Continue with the theory and code index.

8. Linear systems and curvature for policy iteration and TRPO

A linear system Ax=bAx=bAx=b asks for a vector whose matrix product equals bbb. For A=diag⁡(2,4)A=\operatorname{diag}(2,4)A=diag(2,4) and b=(6,8)Tb=(6,8)^Tb=(6,8)T, the solution is (3,2)T(3,2)^T(3,2)T. Numerically solve the system rather than explicitly forming A−1A^{-1}A−1. Policy evaluation solves (I−γPπ)V=rπ(I-\gamma P_\pi)V=r_\pi(I−γPπ​)V=rπ​; each row couples a state's value to expected successor values.

A Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives, Hij=∂2f/(∂θi∂θj)H_{ij}=\partial^2 f/(\partial\theta_i\partial\theta_j)Hij​=∂2f/(∂θi​∂θj​). For f(θ)=θ12+2θ22f(\theta)=\theta_1^2+2\theta_2^2f(θ)=θ12​+2θ22​, it is diag⁡(2,4)\operatorname{diag}(2,4)diag(2,4). Taylor's local quadratic approximation is

f(θ+d)≈f(θ)+∇f(θ)Td+12dTHd.f(\theta+d)\approx f(\theta)+\nabla f(\theta)^Td+\tfrac12d^THd. f(θ+d)≈f(θ)+∇f(θ)Td+21​dTHd.

A symmetric matrix is positive definite if dTHd>0d^THd>0dTHd>0 for every nonzero ddd; positive semidefinite permits zero. KL curvature at equal distributions is semidefinite. Adding ηI\eta IηI, with η>0\eta>0η>0, makes the system easier to solve and handles redundant softmax logit shifts. TRPO solves a curvature system to scale steps according to policy change rather than raw parameter distance. Conjugate gradient approximates such a solve using matrix-vector products, without storing the full matrix. The small TRPO lab forms the matrix explicitly.

00_start/TRICKS_AND_DEBUGGING.md

Practical tricks, with the reason behind each one

Before training

  • Overfit 8–32 examples first. Failure usually means the data, loss, mask, or optimizer is wrong; a larger GPU rarely fixes it.
  • Print decoded inputs and supervised labels. Check EOS, padding, truncation, template boundaries, and whether any response tokens survive.
  • Split by source/document/user before chunking. Overlapping windows from the same document in both splits can create misleading validation scores.
  • Record model revision, tokenizer, template, dataset hash, seed, library versions and configuration. A seed alone does not guarantee reproducibility.
  • Start with a simple baseline and a held-out evaluation set. For RL include a random policy; for offline RL include behavior cloning.

When loss behaves badly

Symptom Likely checks
Loss is NaN Empty supervised masks, invalid log values, excessive LR, FP16 overflow
Loss never changes Frozen parameters, missing backward/step, detached computation
Loss falls but generation is bad Leakage, wrong template, tiny/poor data, wrong task metric
CUDA out of memory Sequence length, activation size, batch size, optimizer state
Training resumes differently Missing RNG/sampler/optimizer/scheduler state
LoRA has no effect Target module names, adapter loading, actual trainable parameters
RL reward suddenly collapses Update size, stale rollouts, incorrect advantage/bootstrap masks
High reward but poor behavior Reward hacking, verifier bugs, evaluation mismatch

Fine-tuning techniques

Use smaller learning rates when modifying pretrained weights. Warmup avoids large early updates; clipping limits large gradients. Neither replaces correct loss scaling. Select learning rate on validation, not a fixed universal rule.

Try data quality and coverage before more epochs. Monitor forgetting on the original capabilities as well as target performance. Increase LoRA rank only when the adaptation capacity appears limiting; compare under a fixed budget.

Use gradient accumulation for larger effective batches, mixed precision for appropriate hardware, and activation checkpointing for long sequences. A 4-bit base still has floating-point activations and adapter optimizer state. Sequence length can dominate memory even when weights are heavily compressed.

RL techniques

Separate training exploration from evaluation. Evaluate without updates and with a defined action-selection rule. Report multiple training seeds and several evaluation episodes per trained agent.

Keep rewards and observations at manageable scales. Fit normalization using training experience and freeze it during evaluation. Reward normalization and reward clipping change optimization; reward clipping can change the task.

For Gymnasium, step returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info). Reset after either end flag. Bootstrap across a time-limit truncation when the underlying task continues, using the final observation before reset; stop the GAE trace at both kinds of episode boundary. See the official API guide.

For PPO, log entropy, value loss, approximate KL, clip fraction, and return. For DQN/SAC, inspect target values, replay diversity, and update-to-data ratio. Small surrogate loss alone does not prove the policy is improving.

Honest experiments

Change one factor at a time. Compare at equal data/compute budgets and keep a final test set untouched. Report failures and confidence intervals along with averages. For repeated tasks from the same source, resample at the source level.

00_start/GLOSSARY.md

Vocabulary beside the code

Term Meaning
Parameter / weight A learned number inside a model
Hyperparameter A choice such as learning rate, rank or batch size
Tensor A multidimensional array with shape and numeric type
Logit Unnormalized score before softmax
Softmax Converts scores into probabilities summing to one
Log-probability Log of a probability; products become sums
Cross-entropy Negative log-probability assigned to the target
Gradient Derivatives of an objective with respect to parameters
Autograd Automatic differentiation using the chain rule
Backpropagation Reverse traversal that computes those derivatives
Optimizer A rule for updating parameters from gradients
AdamW Adaptive gradient optimizer with decoupled weight decay
Epoch / step Pass through data / a training update (check local meaning)
Generalization Performance on unseen data from the intended task
Leakage Evaluation information accidentally entering training/selection
Embedding Learned vector representing a token or other discrete item
Attention Content-dependent weighted aggregation of representations
Causal mask Prevents attending to future positions
Pretraining Initial broad learning, often next-token prediction
SFT Supervised fine-tuning on desired examples
PEFT / LoRA / QLoRA Parameter-efficient tuning / low-rank updates / quantized-base LoRA
Policy pi(a given s) Distribution of actions given state/observation
State / observation Environment's underlying condition / what the agent sees
Reward r Immediate feedback after an action
Return G Sum of future rewards, usually discounted
Discount gamma Weight on future rewards; often between zero and one
V(s) Expected return from a state under a policy
Q(s,a) Expected return after a state/action pair under a policy
Advantage A(s,a) Q(s,a)-V(s): better/worse than the state baseline
TD error Sampled reward plus bootstrap value minus current estimate
Bootstrap Use a learned future estimate in a training target
On-policy Learn from the policy currently being improved
Off-policy Learn a target policy using behavior from another policy
Replay buffer Stored transitions reused for learning
Actor / critic Policy model / value estimator
Entropy Uncertainty of an action distribution
KL divergence Directional measure of difference between distributions
GAE Smoothed sum of temporal-difference errors estimating advantage
RLHF / RLAIF Reinforcement learning using human / AI-derived feedback
DPO Direct preference optimization from chosen/rejected examples
GRPO Group-relative policy optimization using within-prompt rewards
Quantization Represent numbers using fewer bits and scaling/codebooks
Distillation Train a student to approximate a teacher's behavior
Ablation Remove/change one component to test its contribution

Notation: B=batch size, T=sequence length, V=vocabulary size, d=hidden width, r=LoRA rank, alpha=adapter scale (or an unrelated SAC temperature), beta=reference regularization scale. Symbols can mean different things in different algorithms; read each local definition.

Part 1

Foundations

01_foundations/01_python_and_math.md

Python, vectors, softmax, and gradient descent

Companion code: 01_python_and_math.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

What you are learning and why

A model is a parameterized calculation. Training chooses its parameters so predictions match examples. Before a neural network, understand a model with only two learned numbers: y^=wx+b\hat y=wx+by^​=wx+b. Here xxx is an input, www is a slope, and bbb is an offset. The code learns the hidden rule y=2x+3y=2x+3y=2x+3 from five pairs.

Python lists store the examples, a for loop repeats updates, and a function packages a reusable calculation. zip(a, b) pairs corresponding list entries; sum(...) adds them. A list comprehension [f(x) for x in xs] applies a calculation to every item and returns the results as a list.

Vectors and dot products

A scalar is one number; a vector is an ordered list. For vectors of length ddd:

a⋅b=∑j=1dajbj.a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_jb_j. a⋅b=j=1∑d​aj​bj​.

For [1, 2] and [3, 4], this is 1(3)+2(4)=111(3)+2(4)=111(3)+2(4)=11. In a model, the dot product combines input features with their learned weights. A matrix stores several vectors as rows or columns, allowing many dot products in one operation.

Softmax: formula, code, and numerical stability

Logits are arbitrary real scores. To obtain a probability distribution:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑jexp⁡(zj).p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j)}. pi​=∑j​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Exponential makes each term positive, and dividing by their sum makes the probabilities add to one. Higher logits produce higher probabilities. These probabilities are model outputs, not automatically calibrated confidence.

A direct implementation is:

exponentials = [math.exp(score) for score in logits]
denominator = sum(exponentials)
probabilities = [value / denominator for value in exponentials]

The actual softmax function subtracts m=max⁡jzjm=\max_j z_jm=maxj​zj​ first:

ezi−m∑jezj−m=e−mezie−m∑jezj=ezi∑jezj.\frac{e^{z_i-m}}{\sum_j e^{z_j-m}} =\frac{e^{-m}e^{z_i}}{e^{-m}\sum_j e^{z_j}} =\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}. ∑j​ezj​−mezi​−m​=e−m∑j​ezj​e−mezi​​=∑j​ezj​ezi​​.

The common factor cancels, so this is the same formula. But the largest exponential is now e0=1e^0=1e0=1, avoiding overflow from numbers such as e1000e^{1000}e1000. For [1,2,3], exponentiate [-2,-1,0] to get approximately [0.1353,0.3679,1]. Divide by 1.5032 to get [0.0900,0.2447,0.6652]. In the original short function, shifted contains these exponentials, not just the shifted scores. The final list comprehension normalizes them.

For a correct class kkk, negative log-likelihood is −log⁡pk-\log p_k−logpk​. If the correct class has probability 0.6652, the loss is about 0.4076. Giving it probability 0.01 produces loss about 4.6052. Minimizing this loss encourages more probability on the correct class.

Derivatives: which direction reduces error?

Define error ei=wxi+b−yie_i=wx_i+b-y_iei​=wxi​+b−yi​ and mean squared error:

L(w,b)=1N∑iei2.L(w,b)=\frac1N\sum_i e_i^2. L(w,b)=N1​i∑​ei2​.

A derivative measures local change. The chain rule gives:

∂L∂w=2N∑ieixi,∂L∂b=2N∑iei.\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}=\frac2N\sum_i e_ix_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\frac2N\sum_i e_i. ∂w∂L​=N2​i∑​ei​xi​,∂b∂L​=N2​i∑​ei​.

Why? The derivative of ei2e_i^2ei2​ is 2ei2e_i2ei​ times the derivative of eie_iei​; ∂ei/∂w=xi\partial e_i/\partial w=x_i∂ei​/∂w=xi​ and ∂ei/∂b=1\partial e_i/\partial b=1∂ei​/∂b=1.

For the code's five inputs [-2,-1,0,1,2], targets are [-1,1,3,5,7]. At w=b=0w=b=0w=b=0, errors are [1,-1,-3,-5,-7]. Therefore ∂L/∂w=−8\partial L/\partial w=-8∂L/∂w=−8 and ∂L/∂b=−6\partial L/\partial b=-6∂L/∂b=−6.

Gradient descent subtracts the gradient:

w←w−η∂L∂w,b←b−η∂L∂b.w\leftarrow w-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w},\qquad b\leftarrow b-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}. w←w−η∂w∂L​,b←b−η∂b∂L​.

With learning rate η=0.1\eta=0.1η=0.1, the first updated weights are w=0.8w=0.8w=0.8, b=0.6b=0.6b=0.6. The negative gradient means increasing these parameters initially reduces loss. This follows from the local approximation L(θ+Δ)≈L(θ)+∇LTΔL(\theta+\Delta)\approx L(\theta)+\nabla L^T\DeltaL(θ+Δ)≈L(θ)+∇LTΔ: choosing Δ=−η∇L\Delta=-\eta\nabla LΔ=−η∇L predicts a decrease of η∥∇L∥2\eta\|\nabla L\|^2η∥∇L∥2. For too large a step, the approximation can fail and loss may grow.

Connect to the script

Code Meaning
errors = [...] Calculate y^i−yi\hat y_i-y_iy^​i​−yi​
loss = ... / len(xs) Average squared error over examples
dw, db The two derivatives derived above
weight -= learning_rate * dw Gradient descent for the slope
bias -= learning_rate * db Gradient descent for the offset

random.seed(7) has no effect on this deterministic dataset; it is a reproducibility habit for later randomized examples. The code reports loss before its update and weights after its update, so they refer to adjacent points in the training loop.

Run, experiment, and check

Run python 01_foundations/01_python_and_math.py. Expect the dot product 11, softmax probabilities summing to one, and weights approaching 2 and 3. Try y=−3x+1y=-3x+1y=−3x+1; the learned weights should approach -3 and 1. Explain why adding 100 to every logit leaves softmax unchanged. Check the cancellation above. A frequent error is adding the gradient instead of subtracting it: that performs ascent on the loss.

Next: tensors and automatic differentiation.

Companion code: 01_python_and_math.py

01_foundations/01_python_and_math.py

1"""Python and the mathematics hiding inside training.2Run: python3 01_foundations/01_python_and_math.py3Requires: Python only. Read each comment, then change one number and rerun.45A scalar is one number; a vector is a list of numbers; a matrix is a table.6A parameter is a number learned from data. A hyperparameter (e.g. learning7rate) is chosen by us. Loss measures how wrong predictions are.8Exercise: change the target rule to y = -3*x + 1 and recover its parameters.9"""10import math11import random1213# A function packages a reusable calculation. zip pairs corresponding elements.14def dot(a, b):15    assert len(a) == len(b), 'Dot products require matching dimensions.'16    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))171819def softmax(logits):20    # Subtracting the maximum prevents exp(large_number) from overflowing.21    shifted = [math.exp(x - max(logits)) for x in logits]22    return [x / sum(shifted) for x in shifted]232425def main():26    random.seed(7)  # Reproducibility: the same pseudorandom sequence each run.27    print('dot product:', dot([1, 2], [3, 4]))28    probabilities = softmax([1, 2, 3])29    print('probabilities:', probabilities, 'sum:', sum(probabilities))30    # Cross-entropy for a single correct class = -log(probability of that class).31    print('loss when class 2 is correct:', -math.log(probabilities[2]))32    xs = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]33    ys = [2*x + 3 for x in xs]34    weight, bias, learning_rate = 0.0, 0.0, 0.135    for step in range(100):36        errors = [weight*x + bias - y for x, y in zip(xs, ys)]37        loss = sum(e*e for e in errors) / len(xs)38        # Derivatives tell us how loss changes when each parameter changes.39        dw = 2 * sum(e*x for e, x in zip(errors, xs)) / len(xs)40        db = 2 * sum(errors) / len(xs)41        weight -= learning_rate * dw  # Descend: move opposite the gradient.42        bias -= learning_rate * db43        if step % 25 == 0:44            print(f'step={step:3} loss={loss:.6f} w={weight:.3f} b={bias:.3f}')45    assert abs(weight - 2) < 0.01 and abs(bias - 3) < 0.014647if __name__ == '__main__':48    main()
01_foundations/02_tensors_autograd.md

Tensors, automatic differentiation, and checking gradients

Companion code: 02_tensors_autograd.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

The question this example answers

How does PyTorch know which weight changes reduce loss, and how can we check its answer? We compute the same derivative in three ways: by hand, with backward(), and with small numerical perturbations. Then we examine a shape mistake that changes the problem without producing an error.

Read gradient descent first. A tensor is an array with shape, numeric type, and device. requires_grad=True enables derivative tracking for a floating-point tensor. Tracking is different from updating.

Inputs and matrix multiplication

The arrays are:

X=[1234],w=[0.20.3],y=[12].X=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad w=\begin{bmatrix}0.2\\0.3\end{bmatrix},\quad y=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}. X=[13​24​],w=[0.20.3​],y=[12​].

Rows of XXX are examples. Columns are features. There are two weights and no bias in this model. Matrix multiplication gives:

y^=Xw=[1(0.2)+2(0.3)3(0.2)+4(0.3)]=[0.81.8].\hat y=Xw=\begin{bmatrix}1(0.2)+2(0.3)\\3(0.2)+4(0.3)\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}0.8\\1.8\end{bmatrix}. y^​=Xw=[1(0.2)+2(0.3)3(0.2)+4(0.3)​]=[0.81.8​].

The shape rule is [2,2] @ [2,1] -> [2,1]. In Python, @ is matrix multiplication; * would be elementwise multiplication with broadcasting.

Loss and an explicit derivative

L=12[(0.8−1)2+(1.8−2)2]=0.04.L=\frac12[(0.8-1)^2+(1.8-2)^2]=0.04. L=21​[(0.8−1)2+(1.8−2)2]=0.04.

For NNN examples, the gradient of L=∥Xw−y∥2/NL=\|Xw-y\|^2/NL=∥Xw−y∥2/N is:

∇wL=2NXT(Xw−y).\nabla_wL=\frac2N X^T(Xw-y). ∇w​L=N2​XT(Xw−y).

For this batch, Xw−y=[−0.2,−0.2]TXw-y=[-0.2,-0.2]^TXw−y=[−0.2,−0.2]T, so:

∂L∂w1=(−0.2)(1)+(−0.2)(3)=−0.8,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}=(-0.2)(1)+(-0.2)(3)=-0.8, ∂w1​∂L​=(−0.2)(1)+(−0.2)(3)=−0.8,

∂L∂w2=(−0.2)(2)+(−0.2)(4)=−1.2.\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}=(-0.2)(2)+(-0.2)(4)=-1.2. ∂w2​∂L​=(−0.2)(2)+(−0.2)(4)=−1.2.

The graph is w -> predictions -> errors -> squared errors -> mean. Autograd traverses it backwards and multiplies local derivatives using the chain rule. loss.backward() accumulates the resulting derivatives in w.grad, approximately [[-0.8],[-1.2]]. No optimizer is present, so the weights remain unchanged after this call.

analytical = w.grad.clone() saves an independent copy. The name distinguishes this chain-rule derivative from a finite-difference estimate; PyTorch is doing automatic differentiation, not symbolic algebra or finite differences.

Finite differences: measuring a slope without autograd

For a smooth one-variable function:

f′(u)≈f(u+ϵ)−f(u−ϵ)2ϵ.f'(u)\approx\frac{f(u+\epsilon)-f(u-\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}. f′(u)≈2ϵf(u+ϵ)−f(u−ϵ)​.

Taylor expansion gives f(u±ϵ)=f(u)±ϵf′(u)+ϵ2f′′(u)/2±ϵ3f(3)(u)/6+⋯f(u\pm\epsilon)=f(u)\pm\epsilon f'(u) +\epsilon^2f''(u)/2\pm\epsilon^3f^{(3)}(u)/6+\cdotsf(u±ϵ)=f(u)±ϵf′(u)+ϵ2f′′(u)/2±ϵ3f(3)(u)/6+⋯. Subtracting and dividing cancels the even terms, leaving f′(u)+O(ϵ2)f'(u)+O(\epsilon^2)f′(u)+O(ϵ2). Very small ϵ\epsilonϵ can amplify floating-point roundoff; smaller is not always more accurate.

The script holds w2=0.3w_2=0.3w2​=0.3 fixed and perturbs only w1w_1w1​ with ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001ϵ=0.001:

w1w_1w1​ Predictions Mean squared error
0.201 [0.801, 1.803] 0.039205
0.199 [0.799, 1.797] 0.040805

The estimated derivative is (0.039205−0.040805)/0.002=−0.8(0.039205-0.040805)/0.002=-0.8(0.039205−0.040805)/0.002=−0.8. Restoring the original weight is essential: this is a diagnostic, not a training update.

Code Purpose
with torch.no_grad() Avoid recording the diagnostic edits/calculations
w[0,0].item() Read one weight as a Python number
plus, minus Evaluate the loss on either side of the original weight
(plus-minus)/(2*eps) Central finite-difference estimate
allclose(..., atol=1e-3) Compare with absolute tolerance plus default relative tolerance

Why broadcasting can silently break a loss

Correct: predictions and targets both have shape [2,1]. Each prediction is compared with its matching target, giving errors [[-0.2],[-0.2]].

target.squeeze(1) removes its length-one second dimension, producing shape [2]. PyTorch aligns dimensions from the right. [2,1] and [2] broadcast to [2,2], producing all pairwise differences:

[0.8−10.8−21.8−11.8−2]=[−0.2−1.20.8−0.2].\begin{bmatrix}0.8-1&0.8-2\\1.8-1&1.8-2\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2&-1.2\\0.8&-0.2\end{bmatrix}. [0.8−11.8−1​0.8−21.8−2​]=[−0.20.8​−1.2−0.2​].

The wrong mean squared error would be (0.04+1.44+0.64+0.04)/4=0.54(0.04+1.44+0.64+0.04)/4=0.54(0.04+1.44+0.64+0.04)/4=0.54, not 0.04. Always inspect shapes before computing a regression loss.

Run and check understanding

Run python 01_foundations/02_tensors_autograd.py. Expect numerical derivative near -0.8, automatic gradient near [[-0.8],[-1.2]], and shape outputs [2,2] and [2,1]. Independently perturb the second weight: its estimate should be near -1.2. Try eps=0.1 and eps=1e-8; this quadratic has no central-difference truncation error in exact arithmetic, but float32 roundoff can spoil the tiny step.

manual_seed has no effect here because the tensors are explicit constants. set_num_threads affects execution scheduling, not the mathematics. Finally, if __name__ == '__main__': main() runs the demonstration only when the file is executed directly.

Reference: PyTorch automatic differentiation.

Companion code: 02_tensors_autograd.py

01_foundations/02_tensors_autograd.py

1"""Tensor shapes, broadcasting, derivatives, and gradient checks.2Requires: torch. A batch has shape [B, features]; a weight matrix [features, out].3Autograd records operations and applies the chain rule in reverse.4Exercise: deliberately omit zero_grad in 03_neural_network_training.py and observe accumulation.5"""6import torch789def main():10    torch.set_num_threads(1)  # Small examples run faster without large thread pools.11    torch.manual_seed(7)12    x = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])  # Shape [2 examples, 2 features].13    w = torch.tensor([[0.2], [0.3]], requires_grad=True)14    target = torch.tensor([[1.], [2.]])15    loss = ((x @ w - target)**2).mean()16    loss.backward()  # Populates w.grad; it does NOT update w.17    analytical = w.grad.clone()18    # Finite differences independently check a derivative on this tiny problem.19    eps = 1e-320    with torch.no_grad():21        original = w[0, 0].item()22        w[0, 0] = original + eps23        plus = ((x @ w - target)**2).mean()24        w[0, 0] = original - eps25        minus = ((x @ w - target)**2).mean()26        w[0, 0] = original27    numerical = (plus - minus) / (2*eps)28    print('gradient:', analytical.tolist(), 'finite difference:', numerical.item())29    assert torch.allclose(analytical[0, 0], numerical, atol=1e-3)30    # Broadcasting [2,1] against [2] produces [2,2], often a SILENT loss bug.31    print('wrong subtraction shape:', (x @ w - target.squeeze(1)).shape)32    print('correct subtraction shape:', (x @ w - target).shape)3334if __name__ == '__main__':35    main()
01_foundations/03_neural_network_training.md

Neural networks and the complete training loop

Companion code: 03_neural_network_training.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

Why use a neural network?

A linear classifier makes a straight decision boundary. The script labels an example positive when x1x2>0x_1x_2>0x1​x2​>0: both coordinates have the same sign. Positive examples occupy two opposite quadrants. One straight line cannot separate these from the other two quadrants, so we need a nonlinear model.

Prerequisite: tensors and gradients. Our network is:

h=ReLU⁡(W1x+b1),z=W2h+b2.h=\operatorname{ReLU}(W_1x+b_1),\qquad z=W_2h+b_2. h=ReLU(W1​x+b1​),z=W2​h+b2​.

hhh has 32 hidden features; zzz has two class scores. ReLU is max⁡(0,u)\max(0,u)max(0,u) elementwise. It creates different linear behavior in different regions. Without ReLU, composing the layers gives z=W2W1x+W2b1+b2z=W_2W_1x+W_2b_1+b_2z=W2​W1​x+W2​b1​+b2​, still just one affine map.

From scores to a trainable objective

For class kkk, softmax gives pk=ezk/∑jezjp_k=e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}pk​=ezk​/∑j​ezj​. If the correct class is yyy, the per-example loss is:

ℓ=−log⁡py=−zy+log⁡∑jezj.\ell=-\log p_y=-z_y+\log\sum_j e^{z_j}. ℓ=−logpy​=−zy​+logj∑​ezj​.

Differentiating gives a useful identity:

∂ℓ∂zk=pk−1[k=y].\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\mathbf1[k=y]. ∂zk​∂ℓ​=pk​−1[k=y].

For probabilities [0.7,0.3] and correct class 1, gradients on the logits are [0.7,-0.7]. Gradient descent pushes the wrong score down and correct score up. The chain rule then propagates through the output layer, ReLU, and first layer. This is why decreasing cross-entropy encourages correct classification.

cross_entropy(model(inputs), labels) accepts raw logits and integer class indices. It combines log-softmax and negative log-likelihood internally. Passing softmax probabilities instead applies the wrong transformation.

Minibatches, epochs, and AdamW

The empirical objective averages losses across training examples:

L(θ)=1N∑iℓi(θ).L(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_i\ell_i(\theta). L(θ)=N1​i∑​ℓi​(θ).

A shuffled minibatch estimates its gradient using a smaller average. An epoch visits all training examples once. In this file, 400 examples with batch size 32 produce 13 batches, the last one containing 16 examples.

Adam keeps moving averages of gradients and their squares:

mt=β1mt−1+(1−β1)gt,vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2)gt2.m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\quad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2. mt​=β1​mt−1​+(1−β1​)gt​,vt​=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)gt2​.

Bias-corrected versions divide by 1−β1t1-\beta_1^t1−β1t​ and 1−β2t1-\beta_2^t1−β2t​. The adaptive update scales each coordinate roughly by m^t/(v^t+ε)\hat m_t/(\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\varepsilon)m^t​/(v^t​​+ε). AdamW additionally shrinks parameters by a factor approximately 1−ηλ1-\eta\lambda1−ηλ through decoupled weight decay. This discourages unnecessarily large weights; it does not guarantee generalization.

Global gradient clipping replaces ggg by gmin⁡(1,c/∥g∥2)g\min(1,c/\|g\|_2)gmin(1,c/∥g∥2​), with threshold c=1c=1c=1 here. It limits an unusually large gradient before the optimizer uses it.

Map the loop to its purpose

Code Meaning
optimizer.zero_grad(...) Remove gradients left by the previous minibatch
loss.backward() Compute this minibatch's parameter derivatives
clip_grad_norm_ Limit the global gradient norm
optimizer.step() Apply AdamW's update
model.train() Enable training behavior in layers such as dropout
model.eval() and no_grad() Select evaluation behavior and disable graph recording
copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) Preserve the actual best weights, not references to changing tensors

Why separate training, validation, and test data?

The first 400 examples update weights. The next 100 select the stopping point. The final 100 are evaluated once after restoring the best validation checkpoint. This separation reduces optimistic estimates caused by choosing settings on the same examples used to report final quality.

If validation loss fails to improve for eight epochs, training stops. This is patience-based early stopping. Because validation influenced model selection, its score is not an untouched final test result.

Accuracy is the fraction whose largest logit selects the correct class. A model can improve confidence and lower cross-entropy without changing any argmax predictions, so accuracy and loss measure different things.

Run and investigate

Run python 01_foundations/03_neural_network_training.py. Expect falling validation loss and high test accuracy on this easy synthetic task; exact numbers are not universal guarantees. Remove ReLU and explain the remaining classification errors. Reduce training examples and increase width: compare training and validation behavior. Do not repeatedly use the final test split to decide which modification to keep.

Next: tokens and attention.

Companion code: 03_neural_network_training.py

01_foundations/03_neural_network_training.py

1"""A complete supervised training loop with unseen validation data.2An epoch visits the training set once. A minibatch is part of that set.3ReLU supplies nonlinearity; without it, stacked linear layers remain linear.4Train data updates weights; validation selects settings; test data is held5until the final comparison. Never tune repeatedly on the test set.6Exercise: increase width to 256 and shrink training data to see overfitting.7"""8import copy9import torch10from torch import nn11from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset121314def main():15    torch.manual_seed(7)16    torch.set_num_threads(1)17    x = torch.randn(600, 2)18    y = ((x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) > 0).long()  # XOR-like classification.19    train = DataLoader(TensorDataset(x[:400], y[:400]), batch_size=32, shuffle=True)20    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 2))21    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, weight_decay=0.01)22    best_loss, best_state, stale = float('inf'), None, 023    for epoch in range(60):24        model.train()  # Activates dropout / training behavior if present.25        for inputs, labels in train:26            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)27            # CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits, NOT already-softmaxed values.28            loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(inputs), labels)29            loss.backward()30            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)31            optimizer.step()32        model.eval()  # eval() does not disable gradients; no_grad does.33        with torch.no_grad():34            val = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(x[400:500]), y[400:500]).item()35        if val < best_loss:36            best_loss, best_state, stale = val, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()), 037        else:38            stale += 139        if epoch % 10 == 0:40            print(f'epoch={epoch} validation_loss={val:.4f}')41        if stale >= 8:  # Early stopping avoids training past the best validation point.42            break43    model.load_state_dict(best_state)44    with torch.no_grad():45        accuracy = (model(x[500:]).argmax(-1) == y[500:]).float().mean().item()46    print(f'held-out test accuracy: {accuracy:.1%}')4748if __name__ == '__main__':49    main()
01_foundations/04_tokens_attention.md

Tokens, embeddings, and causal attention

Companion code: 04_tokens_attention.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

Why attention is useful

To predict the next token, a model needs context. In “the cat sat,” a prediction may depend on several earlier tokens. Attention lets each position choose a weighted mixture of available contextual representations.

Read softmax first. The script is a mechanics experiment, not a trained language model.

Text becomes discrete IDs, then continuous vectors

For cat sat, the sorted character vocabulary is [' ', 'a', 'c', 's', 't']. The encoded IDs are [2,1,4,0,3,1,4]. IDs are lookup addresses, not numerical measurements: ID 4 is not “twice as meaningful” as ID 2.

An embedding table E∈RV×dE\in\mathbb R^{V\times d}E∈RV×d contains one learned vector per token. Looking up token iii returns row EiE_iEi​. Here V=5V=5V=5 and d=8d=8d=8. During training, gradients update the rows used by examples; the coordinates are learned representations, not predefined linguistic labels.

For next-token prediction, inputs are IDs except the last, while labels are IDs except the first. Position ttt uses context through ttt to predict t+1t+1t+1.

For example, use the character tokens of cat sat, including its space:

ids = [2, 1, 4, 0, 3, 1, 4]  # c a t SPACE s a t
inputs = ids[:-1]             # [2, 1, 4, 0, 3, 1] = "cat sa"
labels = ids[1:]              # [1, 4, 0, 3, 1, 4] = "at sat"

Positions start at zero. Each output predicts the token immediately after its input position, using all allowed context:

Position ttt Input token Allowed context Correct next token
0 c c a
1 a ca t
2 t cat space
3 space cat s
4 s cat s a
5 a cat sa t

At position 4, the model predicts a from cat s. The causal mask prevents it from reading the a at position 5, even though that token is in the input. The model can compute all six predictions in one forward pass with this mask.

For original IDs z0,…,zN−1z_0,\ldots,z_{N-1}z0​,…,zN−1​, the aligned input and target are xt=ztx_t=z_txt​=zt​ and yt=zt+1y_t=z_{t+1}yt​=zt+1​ for t=0,…,N−2t=0,\ldots,N-2t=0,…,N−2. The training objective is:

L=−1N−1∑t=0N−2log⁡pθ(zt+1∣z0,…,zt).\mathcal L=-\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{t=0}^{N-2} \log p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_0,\ldots,z_t). L=−N−11​t=0∑N−2​logpθ​(zt+1​∣z0​,…,zt​).

The last token is excluded from inputs because this sequence provides no following token as its target. The first token is excluded from labels because there is no preceding input position to predict it. Seven tokens therefore provide six input-target pairs. The companion script demonstrates the attention mechanics; it does not train this predictor.

Derive scaled dot-product attention

Let X∈RT×dX\in\mathbb R^{T\times d}X∈RT×d contain one representation per position. A full attention head learns projections:

Q=XWQ,K=XWK,V=XWV.Q=XW_Q,\quad K=XW_K,\quad V=XW_V. Q=XWQ​,K=XWK​,V=XWV​.

A query asks what a position is looking for, a key describes what a position can match, and a value is the information it contributes. Similarity scores are:

Sij=qi⋅kjdk.S_{ij}=\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}. Sij​=dk​​qi​⋅kj​​.

When query and key components are roughly independent, have mean zero, and have unit variance, a dot product of dkd_kdk​ terms has variance roughly dkd_kdk​. Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ keeps score scale more stable across dimensions and helps avoid overly saturated softmax.

To see why, let qqq and kkk be one query and one key, each with dkd_kdk​ coordinates. Their dot product is a sum of coordinate products:

D=q⋅k=∑r=1dkqrkr.D=q\cdot k=\sum_{r=1}^{d_k}q_r k_r. D=q⋅k=r=1∑dk​​qr​kr​.

For the following idealized calculation, assume all coordinates are mutually independent, with E[qr]=E[kr]=0\mathbb E[q_r]=\mathbb E[k_r]=0E[qr​]=E[kr​]=0 and Var⁡(qr)=Var⁡(kr)=1\operatorname{Var}(q_r)=\operatorname{Var}(k_r)=1Var(qr​)=Var(kr​)=1. Unit variance means expected squared deviation from the mean is 1; it does not mean each value is 1. Since the means are zero, E[qr2]=E[kr2]=1\mathbb E[q_r^2]=\mathbb E[k_r^2]=1E[qr2​]=E[kr2​]=1. Each product then has mean zero and variance one:

E[qrkr]=E[qr]E[kr]=0,\mathbb E[q_rk_r]=\mathbb E[q_r]\mathbb E[k_r]=0, E[qr​kr​]=E[qr​]E[kr​]=0,

Var⁡(qrkr)=E[qr2kr2]−(E[qrkr])2=E[qr2]E[kr2]=1.\operatorname{Var}(q_rk_r) =\mathbb E[q_r^2k_r^2]-(\mathbb E[q_rk_r])^2 =\mathbb E[q_r^2]\mathbb E[k_r^2]=1. Var(qr​kr​)=E[qr2​kr2​]−(E[qr​kr​])2=E[qr2​]E[kr2​]=1.

Independent terms have zero covariance, so their variances add:

Var⁡(D)=∑r=1dkVar⁡(qrkr)=dk.\operatorname{Var}(D)=\sum_{r=1}^{d_k}\operatorname{Var}(q_rk_r)=d_k. Var(D)=r=1∑dk​​Var(qr​kr​)=dk​.

For a concrete random example, imagine every coordinate is independently chosen to be −1-1−1 or +1+1+1, each with probability 1/21/21/2. Each coordinate and each product has mean zero and variance one. With dk=4d_k=4dk​=4, one draw could be:

q=[1,−1,1,1],k=[1,1,−1,1],q=[1,-1,1,1],\qquad k=[1,1,-1,1], q=[1,−1,1,1],k=[1,1,−1,1],

D=1−1−1+1=0.D=1-1-1+1=0. D=1−1−1+1=0.

Other draws give dot products of −4,−2,0,2,-4,-2,0,2,−4,−2,0,2, or 444, with probabilities 1/16,4/16,6/16,4/16,1/161/16,4/16,6/16,4/16,1/161/16,4/16,6/16,4/16,1/16, respectively. Across these draws the mean is zero and the variance is:

E[D2]=16+4(4)+6(0)+4(4)+1616=4=dk.\mathbb E[D^2]=\frac{16+4(4)+6(0)+4(4)+16}{16}=4=d_k. E[D2]=1616+4(4)+6(0)+4(4)+16​=4=dk​.

Variance describes the spread across possible draws, not the value of one particular dot product. Its square root, the standard deviation, is dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​. Scaling a random quantity by ccc scales its variance by c2c^2c2:

Var⁡(Ddk)=1dkVar⁡(D)=1.\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{D}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) =\frac{1}{d_k}\operatorname{Var}(D)=1. Var(dk​​D​)=dk​1​Var(D)=1.

Key dimension dkd_kdk​ Raw dot-product standard deviation Divisor Scaled standard deviation
4 2 2 1
64 8 8 1
256 16 16 1

Larger score differences make softmax more extreme. For example, scores [0, 8] give probabilities approximately [0.0003, 0.9997]. Dividing these scores by 8 gives [0, 1], whose probabilities are approximately [0.269, 0.731]. Scaling helps prevent dimension alone from driving softmax toward near-zero and near-one probabilities, where its gradients can be small.

This is a motivation, not a guarantee about learned queries and keys. Their coordinates may be correlated or have different means and variances. In particular, the companion script uses Q=K=XQ=K=XQ=K=X, so a self-dot-product does not satisfy the independent-query-and-key assumption above.

Normalize each row over source positions, then form a weighted sum:

Pij=eSij∑leSil,Oi=∑jPijVj.P_{ij}=\frac{e^{S_{ij}}}{\sum_l e^{S_{il}}},\qquad O_i=\sum_jP_{ij}V_j. Pij​=∑l​eSil​eSij​​,Oi​=j∑​Pij​Vj​.

A two-position worked example

For easy arithmetic, take one-dimensional queries, keys, and values Q=K=V=[1,2]TQ=K=V=[1,2]^TQ=K=V=[1,2]T. Then S=[[1,2],[2,4]]S=[[1,2],[2,4]]S=[[1,2],[2,4]]. At position 0, causal attention allows only position 0, so weights are [1,0] and output is 1. At position 1, softmax of [2,4] is approximately [0.1192,0.8808], giving output 0.1192(1)+0.8808(2)=1.88080.1192(1)+0.8808(2)=1.88080.1192(1)+0.8808(2)=1.8808.

Each row's weights sum to one. Different query positions can produce different mixtures of the same value vectors.

Why the future must be masked

For causal language modeling, position iii may see only j≤ij\le ij≤i:

Sij←−∞when j>i.S_{ij}\leftarrow-\infty\quad\text{when }j>i. Sij​←−∞when j>i.

Because e−∞=0e^{-\infty}=0e−∞=0, future tokens receive zero probability. Without this mask, the model could read the token it is supposed to predict during training. It could appear successful while failing at generation, where that token does not yet exist.

Code Formula/meaning
x @ x.T / sqrt(dimension) Scores with the simplifying choice Q=K=V=XQ=K=V=XQ=K=V=X
triu(diagonal=1) True above the main diagonal: future positions
masked_fill(..., -inf) Eliminate forbidden positions before normalization
.softmax(-1) Normalize over keys for each query row
probabilities @ x Weighted value mixtures

The script's embeddings are randomly initialized and never trained. It also omits learned Q/K/V projections, multiple heads, and position embeddings. Therefore its printed weights demonstrate valid shapes and masking, not meaningful learned language relationships.

Run and check

Run python 01_foundations/04_tokens_attention.py. Expect a [6,8] output and a lower-triangular [6,6] attention matrix with row sums one. Change only the final input vector: earlier outputs must not change. Remove the mask and repeat: earlier outputs can now depend on the changed future token.

Next: a complete tiny transformer. Reference: Attention Is All You Need.

Companion code: 04_tokens_attention.py

01_foundations/04_tokens_attention.py

1"""Token IDs, embeddings, causal attention, and next-token labels.2Real tokenizers usually use subword units; characters make the mechanics clear.3Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V. A causal mask blocks the future.4Exercise: remove the mask and explain why the resulting training task leaks.5"""6import math7import torch8from torch import nn91011def causal_attention(x):12    # Here Q=K=V=x for clarity; a transformer learns separate projections.13    length, dimension = x.shape14    scores = x @ x.T / math.sqrt(dimension)15    future = torch.ones(length, length, dtype=torch.bool).triu(diagonal=1)16    probabilities = scores.masked_fill(future, float('-inf')).softmax(-1)17    return probabilities @ x, probabilities181920def main():21    torch.set_num_threads(1)  # Small examples run faster without large thread pools.22    torch.manual_seed(7)23    text = 'cat sat'24    vocabulary = sorted(set(text))25    token_to_id = {character: index for index, character in enumerate(vocabulary)}26    ids = torch.tensor([token_to_id[c] for c in text])27    embedding = nn.Embedding(len(vocabulary), 8)28    inputs, labels = ids[:-1], ids[1:]  # Each position predicts the next character.29    output, attention = causal_attention(embedding(inputs))30    print('vocabulary:', token_to_id)31    print('input IDs:', inputs.tolist(), 'next-token IDs:', labels.tolist())32    print('attention weights:', attention.detach().round(decimals=2))33    assert torch.all(attention.triu(1) == 0)34    assert torch.allclose(attention.sum(-1), torch.ones(len(inputs)))35    print('output shape:', output.shape)36    # Full transformers also use positional information, multiple heads,37    # residual additions, normalization and feed-forward blocks: see 05_tiny_transformer.py.3839if __name__ == '__main__':40    main()
01_foundations/05_tiny_transformer.md

A tiny transformer language model from start to sampling

Companion code: 05_tiny_transformer.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

The learning objective

This file trains a small character language model from random initialization. It learns one repeated sentence, so it demonstrates pretraining mechanics and memorization, not broad language understanding. Read attention and training loops first.

A causal model factorizes a sequence probability:

pθ(x1,…,xT)=∏t=1Tpθ(xt∣x<t).p_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^Tp_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}). pθ​(x1​,…,xT​)=t=1∏T​pθ​(xt​∣x<t​).

Taking negative logs turns products into sums. The training objective is the average next-token negative log-probability. We can predict every next token in a window in parallel because the causal mask prevents future leakage.

What each part of the architecture contributes

Input token xtx_txt​ becomes ht(0)=E[xt]+P[t]h_t^{(0)}=E[x_t]+P[t]ht(0)​=E[xt​]+P[t]. EEE stores token embeddings; PPP stores learned position embeddings. Adding positions lets the model represent order: the same token at two locations need not have the same input.

The block uses four attention heads. With width 32, each head uses width 8. Independent projected queries/keys/values allow different heads to aggregate different relationships. Head outputs are concatenated and projected back to width 32.

The default encoder layer here uses residual additions and post-layer normalization, with dropout set to zero:

u=LayerNorm⁡(h+MHA⁡(h)),h′=LayerNorm⁡(u+FFN⁡(u)).u=\operatorname{LayerNorm}(h+\operatorname{MHA}(h)),\qquad h'=\operatorname{LayerNorm}(u+\operatorname{FFN}(u)). u=LayerNorm(h+MHA(h)),h′=LayerNorm(u+FFN(u)).

The feed-forward network is W2ReLU⁡(W1u+b1)+b2W_2\operatorname{ReLU}(W_1u+b_1)+b_2W2​ReLU(W1​u+b1​)+b2​, with intermediate width 64. Residual paths make it easier to propagate information and gradients without forcing every block to relearn an identity mapping. Layer normalization standardizes features within a token representation and then applies learned scale and offset; it does not normalize a whole batch.

Although the PyTorch class is named TransformerEncoder, supplying a causal mask makes this use causal self-attention. There is no cross-attention or separate encoder-decoder architecture in this example.

Shapes and loss

Stage Shape
Input IDs [B,T]
Embeddings and block output [B,T,32]
Vocabulary logits [B,T,V]
Flattened logits for cross-entropy [B*T,V]
Flattened next-token labels [B*T]

A sampled batch contains 25 tokens per example. The first 24 are inputs; the last 24, offset by one, are targets. The output projection produces a score for every vocabulary token at every input position.

L=−1BT∑b,tlog⁡pθ(xb,t+1∣xb,≤t).L=-\frac1{BT}\sum_{b,t}\log p_\theta(x_{b,t+1}\mid x_{b,\le t}). L=−BT1​b,t∑​logpθ​(xb,t+1​∣xb,≤t​).

Each of 120 updates uses 16 randomly selected windows. This code has no held-out split, so reported loss measures fitting the repeated training sentence only. If evaluating a larger corpus, split source documents before making overlapping windows; otherwise train and validation can contain nearly identical contexts.

Why generation is sequential

Training knows all target tokens, but generation must create them. Start with a, obtain the last position's logits, sample one token, append it, and repeat. Temperature τ>0\tau>0τ>0 changes the distribution:

pi(τ)=ezi/τ∑jezj/τ.p_i(\tau)=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}. pi​(τ)=∑j​ezj​/τezi​/τ​.

For two logits differing by 2, their probability odds are e2/τe^{2/\tau}e2/τ. At τ=1\tau=1τ=1 the odds are about 7.39; at τ=0.5\tau=0.5τ=0.5 they are about 54.6. Lower temperature sharpens preferences, but cannot make an inaccurate model correct. multinomial samples rather than always taking the largest score.

Only the last 24 tokens are passed back to the model. Their learned positions restart at zero for each window; this is a simple sliding-context demonstration, not a KV-cached long-context implementation. eval() and no_grad() prepare inference behavior and prevent unnecessary backward graphs.

Run and experiment

Run python 01_foundations/05_tiny_transformer.py. Loss should fall and sampled text should resemble the repeated sentence. Try a new starting character and a different temperature. Add a held-out corpus and compare loss: memorizing one sentence does not establish generalization. Check causality by changing a future input ID and confirming earlier logits stay unchanged in evaluation mode.

Reference: original transformer architecture. Next: transfer learning.

Companion code: 05_tiny_transformer.py

01_foundations/05_tiny_transformer.py

1"""Train and sample a tiny causal transformer entirely offline.2This is pretraining from random initialization, NOT fine-tuning a pretrained LLM.3A single repeated sentence demonstrates mechanics, not language competence.4Exercise: use a richer corpus, split it BEFORE making overlapping windows,5and report validation cross-entropy instead of memorization loss.6"""7import torch8from torch import nn91011class TinyLM(nn.Module):12    def __init__(self, vocab_size, width=32, context=24):13        super().__init__()14        self.context = context15        self.tokens = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, width)16        self.positions = nn.Embedding(context, width)17        block = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(width, 4, 64, dropout=0.0, batch_first=True)18        self.blocks = nn.TransformerEncoder(block, num_layers=1, enable_nested_tensor=False)19        self.head = nn.Linear(width, vocab_size)2021    def forward(self, ids):22        length = ids.shape[1]23        x = self.tokens(ids) + self.positions(torch.arange(length, device=ids.device))24        mask = torch.ones(length, length, device=ids.device, dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)25        return self.head(self.blocks(x, mask=mask))262728def main():29    torch.manual_seed(7)30    torch.set_num_threads(1)31    corpus = 'a cat sits on a mat. ' * 4032    chars = sorted(set(corpus))33    encoded = torch.tensor([chars.index(c) for c in corpus])34    model = TinyLM(len(chars))35    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.005)36    for step in range(120):37        starts = torch.randint(len(encoded)-model.context-1, (16,))38        batch = torch.stack([encoded[s:s+model.context+1] for s in starts])39        logits = model(batch[:, :-1])40        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, len(chars)), batch[:, 1:].reshape(-1))41        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)42        loss.backward()43        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)44        optimizer.step()45        if step % 40 == 0:46            print('step:', step, 'training loss:', round(loss.item(), 3))47    model.eval()48    ids = torch.tensor([[chars.index('a')]])49    with torch.no_grad():50        for _ in range(60):51            logits = model(ids[:, -model.context:])[:, -1]52            # Temperature <1 sharpens probabilities; >1 increases randomness.53            next_id = torch.multinomial((logits / 0.8).softmax(-1), 1)54            ids = torch.cat([ids, next_id], dim=1)55    print('sample:', ''.join(chars[i] for i in ids[0].tolist()))5657if __name__ == '__main__':58    main()
Part 2

Fine-tuning

02_finetuning/01_transfer_learning.md

Transfer learning: reuse features, then adapt them

Companion code: 01_transfer_learning.py. Read this explanation before running the code.

What changes when we fine-tune?

Training from scratch initializes parameters without task-specific knowledge. Transfer learning begins with parameters learned on a source task, then adapts them to a target task. The hope is that useful source features reduce target data needs. Transfer can also hurt if the source representation is unsuitable.

The code provides a small, fully local experiment. A backbone maps two input features to 16 hidden features; a head maps those features to two logits.

h=fϕ(x),z=gψ(h),L(ϕ,ψ)=1N∑i−log⁡pϕ,ψ(yi∣xi).h=f_\phi(x),\qquad z=g_\psi(h),\qquad L(\phi,\psi)=\frac1N\sum_i-\log p_{\phi,\psi}(y_i\mid x_i). h=fϕ​(x),z=gψ​(h),L(ϕ,ψ)=N1​i∑​−logpϕ,ψ​(yi​∣xi​).

ϕ\phiϕ names backbone parameters, and ψ\psiψ names head parameters. Read neural-network training for cross-entropy and backpropagation.

Source and target tasks in the script

Source labels are ys=1[x1>0]y_s=\mathbf1[x_1>0]ys​=1[x1​>0]. Target labels are yt=1[x1+0.5x2>0]y_t=\mathbf1[x_1+0.5x_2>0]yt​=1[x1​+0.5x2​>0]. Both depend on similar inputs, but the target boundary is tilted. For input [−0.2,1][-0.2,1][−0.2,1], the source label is 0 while the target label is 1 because −0.2+0.5(1)=0.3>0-0.2+0.5(1)=0.3>0−0.2+0.5(1)=0.3>0.

The script uses the first 300 inputs for training in both phases and the final 100 only for final target evaluation. Source and target training tasks share inputs intentionally; they do not share the held-out evaluation inputs.

The three training phases

  1. Source training: optimize both ϕ\phiϕ and ψs\psi_sψs​ for 100 steps.
  2. Head adaptation: replace the head with randomly initialized ψt\psi_tψt​, freeze ϕ\phiϕ, and train only ψt\psi_tψt​ for 60 steps.
  3. Full adaptation: unfreeze ϕ\phiϕ and train both for 60 steps at a smaller learning rate.

While frozen, the backbone is still evaluated in the forward pass. “Frozen” means no learned parameter update, not that its output is constant for all inputs. The head learns a new decision rule over the existing representation:

ψt←ψt−η∇ψtL,ϕ unchanged.\psi_t\leftarrow\psi_t-\eta\nabla_{\psi_t}L, \qquad \phi\text{ unchanged}. ψt​←ψt​−η∇ψt​​L,ϕ unchanged.

After unfreezing, both derivatives matter. A lower learning rate reduces the size of initial changes to reused features. It is a heuristic to preserve useful structure, not a guarantee against forgetting.

How the code implements the idea

Code Purpose
model[1] = nn.Linear(16, 2) Discard the source decision head and create a target head
p.requires_grad_(False) Exclude backbone parameters from gradient computation
Filter model.parameters() by requires_grad Give the optimizer only the intended parameters
Call fit again after unfreezing Create a new optimizer that includes the newly trainable backbone
with torch.no_grad() on final inputs Evaluate without modifying parameters

Each fit call creates a new AdamW optimizer, so optimizer moments restart at each stage. That is a teaching choice. Some practical workflows preserve or carefully rebuild optimizer state when changing trainable parameter groups.

Model weights and optimizer memory are different

The model stores learned weights and biases. AdamW separately stores a step counter and two moving averages for each parameter it updates. For a scalar parameter with gradient gtg_tgt​, these averages are:

mt=β1mt−1+(1−β1)gt,vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2)gt2.m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2. mt​=β1​mt−1​+(1−β1​)gt​,vt​=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)gt2​.

The first moment mtm_tmt​ tracks the recent gradient direction; the second moment vtv_tvt​ tracks squared gradient magnitude (it is not the centered variance). For tensors, these calculations happen element by element. Both start at zero. AdamW uses bias-corrected versions, m^t=mt/(1−β1t)\hat m_t=m_t/(1-\beta_1^t)m^t​=mt​/(1−β1t​) and v^t=vt/(1−β2t)\hat v_t=v_t/(1-\beta_2^t)v^t​=vt​/(1−β2t​), in its update:

θt=(1−ηλ)θt−1−ηm^tv^t+ϵ.\theta_t=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta_{t-1} -\eta\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon}. θt​=(1−ηλ)θt−1​−ηv^t​​+ϵm^t​​.

Here η\etaη is the learning rate, λ\lambdaλ is weight decay, and ϵ\epsilonϵ is a small positive number for numerical stability. The optimizer therefore uses recent gradient history as well as the current gradient.

For example, take β1=0.9\beta_1=0.9β1​=0.9 and β2=0.999\beta_2=0.999β2​=0.999. If the first gradient is g1=2g_1=2g1​=2, then m1=0.2m_1=0.2m1​=0.2 and v1=0.004v_1=0.004v1​=0.004. If the next gradient is −1-1−1, continuing with that same optimizer gives:

m2=0.9(0.2)+0.1(−1)=0.08,v2=0.999(0.004)+0.001(1)=0.004996.m_2=0.9(0.2)+0.1(-1)=0.08,\qquad v_2=0.999(0.004)+0.001(1)=0.004996. m2​=0.9(0.2)+0.1(−1)=0.08,v2​=0.999(0.004)+0.001(1)=0.004996.

Recreating the optimizer before that second gradient instead gives fresh first-step values m1=−0.1m_1=-0.1m1​=−0.1 and v1=0.001v_1=0.001v1​=0.001. Even with the same model weight and current gradient, the gradient-based update can differ because the history and step counter differ. These numbers are the raw moments, before bias correction.

In this script, the state transitions are:

Stage Model parameters AdamW state
Source training Train backbone and source head Start fresh
Head adaptation Keep learned backbone; replace source head with a random target head Start fresh for target head only
Full adaptation Keep the backbone and the now-trained target head; unfreeze backbone Start fresh for both

Creating a new optimizer does not reinitialize the model. In particular, the third fit call keeps the target head's learned weights but discards its 60 steps of optimizer history. Only the explicit nn.Linear(16, 2) replacement creates a new head with new initial weights.

An alternative at unfreezing is to keep the head optimizer and add the newly trainable backbone with optimizer.add_param_group(...). That retains the head's history while giving the newly added parameters fresh state; learning rates must also be set as intended for each group. Unfreezing alone does not add parameters to an optimizer that excluded them. Replacing a head also requires updating optimizer parameter references: an old optimizer still refers to the old head. Preserving state is a deliberate choice, since source gradient history may not suit a changed target objective.

Freezing parameters is different from freezing BatchNorm statistics

For a vision backbone containing BatchNorm, freezing weights alone does not freeze running statistics; train/eval mode needs separate attention. This small backbone has only a linear layer and ReLU, so that issue is absent here.

BatchNorm normally has two kinds of stored state:

State How it changes
Learned scale γ\gammaγ and shift β\betaβ Gradient-based optimizer updates
Running mean and running variance Updates during forward passes in training mode

Setting requires_grad_(False) stops new gradients for the learned parameters. It does not change the layer's training mode, so BatchNorm can still update its running statistics when the frozen backbone processes a batch. Even torch.no_grad() does not stop those training-mode updates.

For example, suppose a BatchNorm feature has running mean 10. A target batch has mean 20, and BatchNorm momentum is 0.1. A training-mode forward pass updates:

running meannew=0.9(10)+0.1(20)=11.\text{running mean}_{\text{new}}=0.9(10)+0.1(20)=11. running meannew​=0.9(10)+0.1(20)=11.

That change happens even if every backbone parameter is frozen and no optimizer step runs. The running variance updates separately as well. During training, BatchNorm normalizes using the current batch statistics; during evaluation, standard BatchNorm uses the stored running statistics. Thus, the representation at evaluation can change even though the weights did not.

If the intention is to keep both the frozen backbone's parameters and its BatchNorm statistics fixed while training the head, a typical setup is:

for p in backbone.parameters():
    p.requires_grad_(False)

model.train()      # Put the overall model in training mode first.
backbone.eval()    # Then keep the backbone in evaluation mode.
# Train using an optimizer containing only the head parameters.

Calling model.train() again also puts its backbone back into training mode, so reapply backbone.eval() afterward when needed. Conversely, eval() by itself does not disable gradients or freeze parameters. These are separate controls. The example assumes BatchNorm tracks running statistics, its default behavior; evaluation mode also disables dropout in a backbone containing it.

Sometimes adapting BatchNorm statistics to target data is intentional. The choice is whether to retain source statistics or update them using target batches. None of this changes the supplied script: its Linear and ReLU backbone has no running statistics or dropout.

What the result means

Run python 02_finetuning/01_transfer_learning.py. Expect high target accuracy. The file illustrates the mechanics but does not prove transfer helped: there is no matched target-only baseline in its printed result. To test that claim, train a fresh model on the same target data and compare multiple seeds under a fair budget. Also evaluate the source task after adaptation to measure forgetting.

Exercise: train with only 20 target examples. Compare head-only, full adaptation, and scratch training. Predict which has lower variance, then check rather than assuming pretrained features always win.
