Projects and appendices

06_projects/PROJECTS.md

Capstones and thesis experiments

Each project should produce runnable code, a configuration file, a data/split manifest, an evaluation table, and a short report of failures and limitations. Start with the smallest version that answers your question.

1. Full fine-tuning versus LoRA

Question: when does a higher adapter rank improve held-out task performance? Build a small domain-specific instruction dataset with non-overlapping source splits. Compare the unchanged base, full tuning, and LoRA ranks 2/8/16. Keep training data, token budget, and evaluation prompts fixed. Report task accuracy, validation loss, trainable parameters, time, peak memory, and source capability retention. Run multiple seeds. Do not infer quality from loss alone.

Stretch: repeat with QLoRA and separate numerical compression effects from changes in hardware, batch size, and optimizer.

2. DQN versus PPO

Question: how do sample efficiency and stability differ on a small discrete task? First use the chain environment. Then implement a Gymnasium adapter and move to a task such as CartPole. Preserve termination/truncation semantics. Compare at equal environment steps, log learning curves, and evaluate multiple seeds.

Ablations: DQN without replay, DQN without a target network, PPO without entropy, and PPO with different rollout/update ratios. Include a random-action baseline.

3. DPO under preference noise

Question: how robust is preference optimization when pair labels are corrupted? Begin with the categorical DPO lesson. Generate train/validation/test preference pairs from a known utility. Flip 0/10/30 percent of TRAINING labels only. Sweep beta using validation data. Measure held-out preference accuracy, KL to the reference, and whether chosen and rejected probabilities move as expected.

Stretch: use a small language model and examine response-length confounding.

4. GRPO reward design

Question: what happens when a reward is easy to game? Expand the one-token task into generated arithmetic answers. Compare exact correctness rewards with a flawed format/length-based reward. Keep a separate correctness evaluator. Measure true accuracy, reward, diversity, response length, and the fraction of groups with zero reward variance.

Stretch: compare group sizes at equal TOTAL generated-token budgets.

5. Offline RL with missing action coverage

Question: how does dataset coverage change the usefulness of pessimism? Collect fixed chain transitions with different behavior policies. Compare behavior cloning, ordinary offline Q-learning, and the discrete CQL penalty. Use held-out environment evaluation without adding those transitions to training. Plot return against coverage and conservative penalty coefficient.

A report template

  • Research question and testable hypothesis.
  • Baselines and why they are appropriate.
  • Data provenance, split policy, and leakage checks.
  • Exact configuration, versions, hardware, seeds and compute budget.
  • Evaluation protocol with uncertainty and paired comparisons where applicable.
  • Results, representative failures, and alternative explanations.
  • Limitations and the next experiment that could disprove your interpretation.

These are starting experiments, not claims of novel thesis contributions. Check the literature before describing any result as new.

00_start/SOURCES.md

Primary sources for deeper study

These links are references, not runtime dependencies. Online documentation can change; match it to the package version you installed. Implementations here are original teaching examples and deliberately smaller than production trainers.

Foundations and fine-tuning

  • PyTorch autograd tutorial: gradients and computational graphs.
  • Attention Is All You Need: transformer architecture.
  • LoRA paper and PEFT LoRA guide: low-rank adaptation.
  • PEFT quicktour: adapters and pretrained model integration.
  • QLoRA paper and bitsandbytes integration: quantized base-model tuning.

Reinforcement learning

  • Sutton and Barto book, author's site: MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, policy gradients.
  • Gymnasium basic usage: reset/step API and episode boundaries.
  • DQN paper: deep Q-learning.
  • Double DQN paper: reducing overestimation.
  • GAE paper: advantage estimation.
  • PPO paper: clipped policy optimization.
  • SAC documentation: entropy-regularized continuous control.
  • CQL paper: conservative offline Q-learning.

Alignment

  • InstructGPT paper: instruction tuning and human feedback.
  • DPO paper and TRL DPO documentation: direct preference optimization.
  • DeepSeekMath paper and TRL GRPO documentation: group-relative policy optimization and implementation variants.

Suggested paper-reading order: problem -> objective equation -> assumptions -> algorithm -> experiments -> limitations. Reproduce one equation before reading all implementation details. The advanced roadmap names further topics without claiming that this folder implements them all.

Additional requested methods

  • A3C: asynchronous advantage actor-critic.
  • TRPO: constrained policy updates.
  • SDPO, v1: feedback-conditioned self-teacher, reverse-KL objective.
  • OPSD, v1: privileged reference context and on-policy distillation.
  • Self-Distilled RLVR / RLSD, v1: verifier advantages with teacher-weighted token credit.

These versioned research references were checked on 2026-10-22. The companion objective labs state their divergence choices and do not reproduce full trainers.

VERIFICATION.md

Verification record

Verified on 2026-09-23 using Python 3.12.3 on CPU. Packages: PyTorch 2.14.0+cpu, NumPy 2.5.3, Transformers 5.17.0, PEFT 0.21.0, Accelerate 1.15.0, and Safetensors 0.8.0. See requirements-tested.txt for top-level version pins. The broader requirements ranges are convenience ranges, not a guarantee that every possible combination has been tested.

Executed successfully

  • All 27 lesson scripts passed Python syntax compilation.
  • python run_lessons.py: 24/24 offline single-process lessons completed.
  • python -m unittest discover -s tests -v: 13/13 numerical checks passed.
  • Two CPU processes ran the DDP lesson successfully. Learned regression weights were approximately [0.999, 0.999, 1.001, 0.997], against a target of all ones.
  • The real-model SFT script loaded sshleifer/tiny-gpt2, ran five LoRA updates, evaluated the validation split, and saved the adapter and tokenizer.
  • The saved LoRA adapter was reloaded with its original base and generated text.
  • The full fine-tuning branch ran two updates, saved a full model checkpoint, and successfully reloaded it for generation.

The numerical tests cover future-token leakage, prompt/padding supervision, LoRA initialization and merging, Bellman values, discounted returns, terminal versus truncated GAE behavior, DPO gradient direction, masked sequence log-probabilities, constant-reward GRPO, conservative Q gradients, and preserving real EOS targets when EOS is also the padding token.

Limits of this verification

These are execution and mathematical-invariant checks, not benchmark claims. The tiny GPT-2 model produced repetitive text and its validation loss did not improve in the short test. That is expected for a plumbing check and is not a useful assistant. The larger default distilgpt2 model was not downloaded/tested.

CUDA mixed precision, NVIDIA QLoRA, large models, multi-GPU training, and other package versions were not tested. SAC/CQL and the categorical alignment labs teach objectives; they are not complete large-scale training systems.

DDP initially could not open local sockets in the restricted execution sandbox; it passed when run with local socket access. Package/model downloads likewise needed network access. Core lessons run offline after installing dependencies.

Checked all 27 companion files exist, all local Markdown links resolve, and fenced code/display-equation delimiters are balanced. Independently recomputed the worked GAE recurrence and return targets, PPO clipping table, finite-difference gradient, broadcasting-error loss, categorical RLHF optimum, and DPO example. These checks passed. They are arithmetic/document-structure checks, not a claim that every Markdown viewer renders LaTeX identically.
